nodes.name: RBF interpolant
nodes.statement: I_{\phi} f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^N c_k \phi(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_k\|) + c_{N+1}.

nodes.name: RBF interpolation linear system
nodes.statement: \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \phi(r_{1,1}) & \phi(r_{1,2}) & \hdots & \phi(r_{1,N}) & 1 \\ \phi(r_{2,1}) & \phi(r_{2,2}) & \hdots & \phi(r_{2,N}) & 1\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\ \phi(r_{N,1}) & \phi(r_{N,2}) & \hdots & \phi(r_{N,N}) & 1\\ 1 & 1 & \hdots & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{A_X} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_N \\ c_{N+1} \end{bmatrix}}_{c_f} = \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} f_1 \\ f_2 \\ \vdots \\ f_N\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{f_X},

nodes.name: Surface / manifold
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we will use the terms surface or manifold to refer to smooth embedded submanifolds of codimension one in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with no boundary, with the specific case of $d = 3$.
nodes.genus: smooth embedded submanifolds of codimension one in $\mathbb{R}^d$

nodes.name: Kernel on Omega
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, and $\phi :\Omega \times\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a kernel with the property $\phi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) := \phi(\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|)$ for $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\Omega$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the standard Euclidean norm in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.name: Radial kernel
nodes.statement: We refer to kernels with this property as \emph{radial kernels} or \emph{radial functions}.

nodes.name: RBF interpolant
nodes.statement_short: RBF interpolant of $f$ on nodes $X$: a linear combination of shifted radial kernels plus a constant.

nodes.name: RBF interpolation linear system
nodes.statement_short: Interpolation and zero-sum conditions give a saddle-point linear system $A_X c_f = f_X$.

nodes.name: Invertibility of RBF interpolation matrix
nodes.statement: If $\phi$ is a positive-definite radial kernel or an order one conditionally positive-definite kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, and all nodes in $X$ are distinct, then the matrix $A_{X}$ above is guaranteed to be invertible (see, for example,~\cite[Ch.\ 6--8]{Wendland:2004}).
assumptions: $\phi$ is a positive-definite radial kernel or an order one conditionally positive-definite kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$
conclusions: the matrix $A_{X}$ above is guaranteed to be invertible

nodes.name: Vector RBF interpolant
nodes.statement: For this problem, we simply apply scalar RBF interpolation as given in Equation \eqref{eq:srbfinterp} to each component of $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})$ and represent the resulting interpolant as $I_{\Phi}\mathbf{g}$.

nodes.name: Vector interpolant in three dimensions
Optimal kernel choice
nodes.statement: It is still an open question as to which kernel is optimal for which application.

nodes.name: Gaussian, multiquadric and inverse multiquadric kernels
nodes.statement: Typically infinitely smooth kernels such as the Gaussian ($\phi(r) = \exp(-(\varepsilon r)^2))$, multiquadric ($\phi(r) = \sqrt{1 + (\varepsilon r)^2}$), and inverse multiquadric ($\phi(r) = 1/\sqrt{1 + (\varepsilon r)^2}$) are used in the RBF-FD method for numerically solving PDEs~\cite{ShuDing2003,Wright200699,Bayona2010,Davydov2011,FlyerLehto2012}.
nodes.origin_citation: Shu & Ding 2003; Wright 2006; Bayona 2010; Davydov 2011; Flyer & Lehto 2012

nodes.name: Shape parameter
nodes.statement: All infinitely smooth kernels, features a free ``shape parameter'' $\varepsilon$, which can be used to change the kernels from peaked (large $\varepsilon$) to flat (small $\varepsilon$).

nodes.name: Flat limit of RBF interpolants
nodes.statement: In the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$ (i.e. a flat kernel), RBF interpolants to data scattered in $\mathbb{R}^d$ typically (and always in the case of the Gaussian radial kernel) converge to (multivariate) polynomial interpolants~\cite{DriscollFornberg2002,LarFor05,Sch05}, and, in the case of the surface of a sphere, they converge to spherical harmonic interpolants~\cite{FoPi07}.
nodes.origin_citation: Driscoll & Fornberg 2002; Larsson & Fornberg 2005; Schaback 2005; Fornberg & Piret 2007
assumptions: In the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$ (i.e. a flat kernel)
conclusions: RBF interpolants to data scattered in $\mathbb{R}^d$ typically (and always in the case of the Gaussian radial kernel) converge to (multivariate) polynomial interpolants~\cite{DriscollFornberg2002,LarFor05,Sch05}
in the case of the surface of a sphere, they converge to spherical harmonic interpolants~\cite{FoPi07}
nodes.statement_short: As $\varepsilon\to0$, RBF interpolants tend to polynomial interpolants (spherical harmonics on the sphere).

nodes.name: Small shape parameters improve accuracy
nodes.statement: For smooth target functions, smaller (but non-zero) values of $\varepsilon$ generally lead to more accurate RBF interpolants~\cite{FoWr,LarFor05}.

nodes.name: Tangent-plane projection operator
nodes.statement:
Let ${ \mathcal P}$ denote the projection operator that takes an arbitrary vector field in $\mathbb{R}^3$ at a point
$\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)$ on the surface and projects it onto the tangent
plane to the surface at $\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Projection operator in terms of the unit normal
nodes.statement:
Letting $\mathbf{n}=(n^x,n^y, n^z)$ denote
the \emph{unit} normal vector to the surface at $\mathbf{x}$, this
operator is given by

\begin{align}
{ \mathcal P} = { \mathcal I} - \mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{T} =
\begin{bmatrix}
(1 - n^x n^x) & -n^x n^y & -n^x n^z  \\
-n^x n^y & (1 - n^y n^y) & -n^y n^z \\
-n^x n^z & -n^y n^z & (1-n^z n^z) 
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{p}^x & 
\mathbf{p}^y &
\mathbf{p}^z 
\end{bmatrix}, \end{align}

where ${ \mathcal I}$ is the $3$-by-$3$ identity matrix, and $\mathbf{p}^x$, $\mathbf{p}^y$ and $\mathbf{p}^z$
are vectors representing the projection operators in the $x$, $y$ and $z$
directions, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: The projection is $\mathcal P = \mathcal I - \mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^T$, with columns $\mathbf{p}^x,\mathbf{p}^y,\mathbf{p}^z$.

nodes.name: Surface gradient operator
nodes.statement:
We can combine ${ \mathcal P}$ with the standard
gradient operator in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\nabla
= \begin{bmatrix} \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \end{bmatrix}^T$, to define
the \emph{surface} gradient operator $\nabla_{\mathbb{M}}$ in Cartesian
coordinates as

\begin{align}
\nabla_{\mathbb{M}} := { \mathcal P}\nabla = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}^x \cdot \nabla \\ \mathbf{p}^y \cdot \nabla \\ \mathbf{p}^z \cdot \nabla \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} { \mathcal G}^x \\ { \mathcal G}^y \\ { \mathcal G}^z \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Surface Laplacian (Laplace-Beltrami operator)
nodes.statement_short: Surface Laplacian as surface divergence of surface gradient: $\mathcal G^x\mathcal G^x+\mathcal G^y\mathcal G^y+\mathcal G^z\mathcal G^z$.

nodes.name: Node set and sampled function
nodes.statement: Let $X = \{\mathbf{x}_k\}_{k=1}^N$ denote a set of (scattered) node locations on a surface $\mathbb{M}$ of dimension two embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and suppose $f:\mathbb{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is some differentiable function sampled on $X$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian

nodes.name: Stencil size n and nearest neighbors
nodes.statement:
Without loss of generality,
let the node where we want to approximate $\Delta_{\mathbb{M}}f$ be
$\mathbf{x}_1$, and let $\mathbf{x}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_n$ be the $n-1$ nearest
neighbors to $\mathbf{x}_1$, measured by Euclidean distance in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian

nodes.name: Stencil
nodes.statement: We refer to $\mathbf{x}_1$ and its $n-1$ nearest neighbors as the \emph{stencil} on the surface corresponding to $\mathbf{x}_1$ and denote this stencil as $P_1 = \{\mathbf{x}_k\}_{k=1}^n$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian

nodes.name: RBF-FD weights
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: RBF-FD weights $w_j$ approximate $\Delta_{\mathbb{M}} f(\mathbf{x}_1)$ as a linear combination of stencil values.

nodes.name: RBF-FD discretization of the surface Laplacian
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
output: a \emph{sparse} $N$-by-$N$ differentiation matrix $L_X$ for approximating the surface Laplacian over all the nodes in $X$
nodes.statement_short: Per stencil: local RBF interpolation, surface-gradient differentiation matrices, their composition into $L_{P}$, keep the center row; assemble sparse $L_X$.

nodes.name: Local RBF interpolation on the stencil
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate $f$ over the stencil $P_1$ by solving $A_{P_1}c_f=f_{P_1}$.

nodes.name: Surface-gradient differentiation matrices
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the interpolant with $\mathcal G^{x,y,z}$ at the stencil nodes, giving $G_{P_1}^{x,y,z}=B_{P_1}A_{P_1}^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Compose gradients into the local Laplacian
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Form $L_{P_1}=G^xG^x+G^yG^y+G^zG^z$.

nodes.name: Extract the center-row weights
nodes.statement: While the approximation in Equation \eqref{eq:surface_lap_P1} is for all the nodes in $P_1$,  we are only interested in the approximation at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_1$ (the ``center'' point of the stencil $P_1$) according to Equation \eqref{eq:fd_weights}.  Because of the ordering of nodes in $P_1$, the value of Equation \eqref{eq:fd_weights} is given by the first value in the vector that results from the product on the right of Equation \eqref{eq:surface_lap_P1}.  Thus, the weights $w_j$ in Equation \ref{eq:fd_weights} are given by the entries in the first row of the matrix $L_{P_1}$ from Equation \eqref{eq:surface_lap_P1}.  Extracting these entries from this matrix, and disregarding the rest, then completes the steps for determining the RBF-FD weights for the node $\mathbf{x}_1$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Keep the first row of $L_{P_1}$ as the weights at $\mathbf{x}_1$.

nodes.name: Repeat per node and assemble L_X
nodes.statement: For each node $\mathbf{x}_j\in X$, $j=1,\ldots,N$, we repeat the above procedure of finding its $n-1$ nearest neighbors (stencil $P_j$), computing the corresponding matrix $L_{P_j}$ according to Equation \eqref{eq:surface_lap_P1}, and extracting out of this matrix the row of RBF-FD weights for $\mathbf{x}_j$.  These weights are then arranged into a \emph{sparse} $N$-by-$N$ differentiation matrix $L_X$ for approximating the surface Laplacian over all the nodes in $X$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: Repeat for every node's stencil and place the weight rows into sparse $L_X$.

nodes.name: Local differentiation matrix G^x_{P_1}
nodes.statement: Here $G_{P_1}^x$ is an $n$-by-$n$ differentiation matrix that represents the RBF approximation to the $x$-component of the surface gradient operator over the set of nodes in $P_1$.

nodes.name: Equivalence to repeated interpolation and differentiation
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
nodes.statement_short: $L_{P_1}$ amounts to interpolate, take surface gradient, re-interpolate, take surface divergence.

nodes.name: No derivatives of normals needed
nodes.statement: This approach of repeated interpolation and differentiation avoids the need to analytically differentiate the surface normal vectors of $\mathbb{M}$, which implies closed form expressions for these values are not needed. This simplifies the computations and makes the method applicable to surfaces defined by point clouds (as illustrated in Section \ref{sec:results2}).
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian

nodes.name: Global RBF-FD differentiation matrix L_X
nodes.statement: These weights are then arranged into a \emph{sparse} $N$-by-$N$ differentiation matrix $L_X$ for approximating the surface Laplacian over all the nodes in $X$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian

nodes.name: Cost of computing RBF-FD weights
nodes.statement: The computational cost of computing each matrix $L_{P_j}$ is $O(n^3)$, and there are $N$ such stencils, so that the total cost of computing the entries of $L_X$ is $O(n^3 N)$ (this is apart from the cost of determining the stencil nodes, for which an efficient method is discussed below).   In practice, $n << N$ and would typically be fixed as $N$ increases, so that the total cost scales like $O(N)$.
nodes.section: 4 RBF-FD approximation to the surface Laplacian
assumptions: In practice, $n << N$ and would typically be fixed as $N$ increases
conclusions: the total cost of computing the entries of $L_X$ is $O(n^3 N)$
the total cost scales like $O(N)$

nodes.name: Total cost of building L_X
nodes.statement: Combining the computational cost of the k-d tree construction and look-ups with computing the RBF-FD weights, the total cost of building $L_X$ is $O(N \log N) + O(N)$, where the constants in the last term depend on the cube of $n$.
conclusions: the total cost of building $L_X$ is $O(N \log N) + O(N)$

nodes.statement_short: Replace $\Delta_{\mathbb{M}}$ by $L_X$ to get $N$ coupled ODEs, then advance in time with a stable integrator.

nodes.name: Semi-discretize in space

nodes.name: Time integration
nodes.statement: This is a (sparse) system of $N$ coupled ODEs and, provided it is stable (see Section \ref{sec:stability}), can be advanced in time with a suitably chosen time-integration method.

nodes.name: RBF-FD surface Laplacian of 1D-surface method
nodes.statement: In that work, given a set of $N$ nodes ($X$) on a surface, we start by using $n$-node RBF-FD formulas to construct differentiation matrices for the ${ \mathcal G}^x$ and ${ \mathcal G}^y$ over the node set $X$, which we denote by $G^x_X$ and $G^y_X$.  Next, the surface Laplacian was approximated from these matrices as $L_X =  G^x_X G^x_X + G^y_X G^y_X$.

nodes.name: Instability of the earlier approach on 2D surfaces
nodes.statement: We tried extending this approach to two dimensional surfaces in embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$, but encountered stability issues when combining this with the method-of-lines, as the differentiation matrices $L_X$ had eigenvalues with (sometimes large) positive real parts.

nodes.name: Necessary eigenvalue condition for MOL stability
nodes.statement: A necessary condition for stability of the MOL approach described in the previous section is that the eigenvalues of the RBF-FD differentiation matrices $L_X$ must be in the stability domain of the ODE solver used for advancing the system in time.  As a minimum requirement, this will generally mean that all eigenvalues must, at the very least, be in the left half plane.
conclusions: the eigenvalues of the RBF-FD differentiation matrices $L_X$ must be in the stability domain of the ODE solver used for advancing the system in time

nodes.name: Flyer-Lehto shape parameter scaling
nodes.statement: It is a generalization of the method from~\cite{FlyerLehto2012} for the surface of the sphere, where the nodes $X$ are quasi-uniformly distributed so that one shape parameter gives roughly equal condition numbers amongst all the stencil interpolation matrices.  In that study, the shape parameter is chosen to be proportional to $\sqrt{N}$, which keeps all the conditions number approximately equal as $N$ grows.

nodes.name: Fill distance
nodes.statement: The convergence of our method is a function of the fill distance $h_X$, defined as the radius of the largest ball that is completely contained on the manifold which does not contain a node in $X$.

nodes.name: Fill distance scaling for quasi-uniform nodes
nodes.statement: For quasi-uniformly distributed nodes on our test surfaces, we expect that $h \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$, where $N$ is the total number of nodes on the surface.
assumptions: quasi-uniformly distributed nodes on our test surfaces
conclusions: $h \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$

nodes.statement: This test problem was presented in \cite{MacDonaldRuuth2009}, and involves solving the heat equation on a unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$. nodes.name: Staggered torus node set generation
nodes.statement:
The node sets we use for experiments on the torus are generated from a ``staggered'' grid in intrinsic variable space, and are determined as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Given $m$, choose $m+1$ equally spaced angles on $[-\pi,\pi]$ in $\varphi$ and $3m+1$ equally spaced angles on $[-\pi,\pi]$ in $\lambda$.
\item Disregard the values of $\varphi$ and $\lambda$ at $\pi$ and take a direct product of the remaining points to obtain $N = 3m^2$ points on $[-\pi,\pi)^2$. Map these points to $\mathbb{T}$ using Equation \eqref{eq:torus} and call the set of nodes $X_1$.
\item Next, generate another set of $N=3m^2$ gridded points in $[-\pi,\pi)^2$ from the previous set by offsetting the $\varphi$ coordinate by $\pi/m$ and the $\lambda$ coordinate by $\pi/(3m)$, so they lie at the midpoints of the previous gridded values. Map these to $\mathbb{T}$ and call the set of nodes $X_2$.
\item The final set of nodes is given by $X=X_1 \cup X_2$.

output: The final set of nodes is given by $X=X_1 \cup X_2$.

nodes.name: Point-cloud preprocessing for general surfaces
nodes.statement: To prepare these point sets for simulations, we first run the Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm~\cite{Kazhdan:2006} to generate a water-tight implicit surface that fits the point cloud. This algorithm requires both the point cloud and the approximate normals as input. Forming an implicit surface smoothes the approximate normal vectors input into the Poisson surface reconstruction, resulting in a more stable RBF-FD discretization. Having generated an implicit surface, we sample that with the Poisson disk sampling algorithm to generate a point cloud with the desired number of points.
